A combination panel answers a comparison from three angles side by side: a **bar chart** of the group means with error bars, a **beeswarm** exposing every individual observation, and a **paired line plot** tracing each subject across the two conditions. Reading them together distinguishes what a single summary hides — an apparent mean difference can come from a consistent shift of every subject or from a few large responders, and only the paired panel shows which. This tutorial reproduces the chart type covered by the *顶刊图社* series (issue 006); see the Reference section below.

## Example

![](../images/Clinics/CombinationPanel_demo.png){fig-alt="CombinationPanel DEMO" fig-align="center" width="95%"}

This combination panel analyses the classic `sleep` study (10 patients, two sleeping drugs, paired design). Panel **a** shows the mean extra sleep per drug with standard-error bars; panel **b** plots every patient's result as a beeswarm; panel **c** connects each patient's two measurements — the upward slopes show that most patients slept longer on Drug 2, exactly the paired evidence the means alone cannot provide.

## Setup

-   System Requirements: Cross-platform (Linux/MacOS/Windows)

-   Programming Language: R

-   Dependencies: `tidyverse`; `ggbeeswarm`; `patchwork`

```{r packages setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, output=FALSE}
# Installing necessary packages
if (!requireNamespace("tidyverse", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("tidyverse")
}
if (!requireNamespace("ggbeeswarm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("ggbeeswarm")
}
if (!requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("patchwork")
}

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(ggbeeswarm)
library(patchwork)
```

## Data Preparation

The example uses the base R `sleep` dataset: paired measurements of extra sleep for 10 patients under two drugs — one row per patient per condition, which is exactly the long shape all three panels need.

```{r load data, message=FALSE}
data("sleep")

sleep_data <- sleep |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, labels = c("Drug 1", "Drug 2")),
         ID = factor(ID))

head(sleep_data, 4)
```

The three panels share one y range so they can be read against each other; fixing it up front avoids three different automatic scales.

```{r shared scales, message=FALSE}
panel_colors <- c("Drug 1" = "#3a86ff", "Drug 2" = "#f4a261")
panel_theme <- theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))
shared_range <- coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.6, 5.8))

summary_stats <- sleep_data |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(mean_extra = mean(extra), se = sd(extra) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")
```

## Visualization

### 1. The Three Panels

Each panel is an ordinary ggplot; `patchwork` composes them with `+` and adds panel tags. The bar panel draws the mean with an error bar, the beeswarm panel needs `ggbeeswarm`, and the pairing panel adds `group = ID` to connect each patient's two points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.1ComboPanels
#| fig-cap: "Bar, beeswarm and paired line panels of the sleep study"
#| out.width: "100%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

panel_a <- ggplot(summary_stats, aes(group, mean_extra, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = .6, colour = "grey20", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_extra - se, ymax = mean_extra + se),
                width = .18, linewidth = .5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = panel_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Extra sleep (h)", title = "Group means ± SE") +
  panel_theme + shared_range

panel_b <- ggplot(sleep_data, aes(group, extra, colour = group)) +
  geom_beeswarm(cex = 1.6, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = panel_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Extra sleep (h)", title = "Individuals") +
  panel_theme + shared_range

panel_c <- ggplot(sleep_data, aes(group, extra, group = ID)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey55", linewidth = .45) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = group), size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = panel_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Extra sleep (h)", title = "Paired slopes") +
  panel_theme + shared_range

panel_a + panel_b + panel_c + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")
```

::: callout-tip
**Key Parameters: **

- `group = ID` in the pairing panel: what switches a scatter into a slope chart; keep one row per subject per condition.
- `coord_cartesian(ylim = ...)`: crops the view without dropping data — use it to give all panels the same range.
- `patchwork`: compose with `+` (side by side) or `plot_layout(ncol = 1)` (stacked); `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")` adds the panel letters.
:::

### 2. Vertical Stack with a Paired Test

Stacking the panels vertically suits narrow figures, and the paired design allows the matching test to be reported right on the slope panel. Note the R idiom: `t.test()` cannot combine a formula with `paired = TRUE` — pass the two vectors instead.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.2StackedCombo
#| fig-cap: "Stacked combination panel with a paired t-test annotation"
#| out.width: "60%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 10

wide <- sleep_data |>
  select(ID, group, extra) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = extra)
paired_test <- t.test(wide[["Drug 2"]], wide[["Drug 1"]], paired = TRUE)
test_label <- sprintf("paired t-test: p = %.3f, mean diff = %.2f h",
                      paired_test$p.value, paired_test$estimate)

panel_c2 <- panel_c +
  labs(title = NULL) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 5.6, label = test_label, size = 3.2)

panel_a + panel_b + panel_c2 +
  plot_layout(ncol = 1) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a")
```

### 3. Highlighting the Mean Trajectory

Adding the mean trajectory on top of the individual slopes separates the group-level shift from the individual scatter — the bold line is the story, the thin lines are the evidence behind it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.3MeanTrajectory
#| fig-cap: "Paired slopes with the mean trajectory highlighted"
#| out.width: "70%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5

panel_c +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line",
               colour = "grey10", linewidth = 1.1) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "point",
               shape = 18, size = 3.2, colour = "grey10") +
  labs(title = "Mean trajectory (bold)")
```

## Applications

-   **Paired clinical designs**: before/after treatment, matched case-control, crossover trials.
-   **Any two-condition comparison**: panels a–c together pre-empt the usual reviewer requests (variability, outliers, pairing).
-   **Reporting**: the annotation ties the visual to the test instead of leaving the statistics implicit.
-   The composition is plain patchwork — each panel can be swapped for a boxplot, density or any other summary without touching the others.
